intro: A reader's guide to signature doctrines and tests, each attributed to the Justice who authored the leading opinion that established it, so it is visible how different rules of American constitutional and procedural law came from different Justices of the Supreme Court. Every case, citation, year, and author below was verified against the U.S. Reports and standard case databases before being written here.

entries.held: Writing for the Court, Ginsburg identified three factors that typically inform whether judicial estoppel bars a party from taking a position contrary to one it previously advanced: (1) the party's later position is clearly inconsistent with its earlier one; (2) the party succeeded in persuading a court to accept the earlier position, so that accepting the inconsistent later position would create the perception that a court was misled; and (3) the party would derive an unfair advantage or impose an unfair detriment on the opponent if not estopped.

entries.doctrine: Thermal-imaging of a home as a Fourth Amendment search
entries.held: Using sense-enhancing technology not in general public use to obtain information about a home's interior that could not otherwise be known without physical intrusion is a search that presumptively requires a warrant.

entries.doctrine: The property-based (trespass) test for Fourth Amendment searches
entries.held: A physical intrusion onto a constitutionally protected area to obtain information is itself a search, restoring the common-law trespass test as a basis for the Fourth Amendment in addition to Katz's reasonable-expectation-of-privacy inquiry (extended to the home's curtilage in Florida v. Jardines, 569 U.S. 1 (2013)).

entries.doctrine: The Confrontation Clause and testimonial statements
entries.held: Testimonial out-of-court statements may not be admitted against a criminal defendant unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine, replacing the prior 'indicia of reliability' approach of Ohio v. Roberts.

entries.doctrine: The tripartite framework for evaluating presidential power
entries.case: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
entries.held: In his concurrence, Jackson set out three zones of executive authority: it is at its maximum when the President acts with congressional authorization, in a 'zone of twilight' when Congress is silent, and at its 'lowest ebb' when the President acts against Congress's expressed or implied will — the now-standard framework for judging executive action.

entries.doctrine: The 'actual malice' standard in defamation law
entries.case: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
entries.held: A public official may not recover damages for defamation relating to official conduct unless the statement was made with 'actual malice' — knowledge that it was false or reckless disregard of whether it was false.

entries.doctrine: Substantive due process as a 'living tradition'
entries.held: In dissent, Harlan argued that the Fourteenth Amendment's liberty is a rational continuum defined by the balance the country has struck between liberty and organized society — a 'living' tradition that both builds on and departs from history — an approach later adopted as the method for identifying unenumerated substantive-due-process rights.

entries.doctrine: The 'undue burden' standard for abortion regulation
entries.case: Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey
entries.held: In the controlling joint plurality opinion, O'Connor (with Kennedy and Souter) reaffirmed the core of Roe v. Wade and held that a pre-viability abortion regulation is invalid if it has the purpose or effect of placing a substantial obstacle — an 'undue burden' — in the path of a woman seeking an abortion. (Casey was later overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022).)

entries.doctrine: The diversity rationale for race-conscious admissions
entries.case: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
entries.held: Powell's controlling opinion held that fixed racial quotas in admissions are unconstitutional, but that the educational benefits of a diverse student body are a compelling interest that may justify considering race as one factor among many. (This rationale was later held not to satisfy strict scrutiny in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023).)

Before custodial interrogation, police must warn a suspect of the right to remain silent, that statements can be used against them, and of the right to counsel (appointed if necessary); statements obtained without these warnings are presumptively inadmissible under the Fifth Amendment.

It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is; the federal courts have the power to declare an act of Congress void when it conflicts with the Constitution.

Harlan's concurrence supplied the enduring two-part test for a Fourth Amendment search: a person must have exhibited an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy, and that expectation must be one society is prepared to recognize as reasonable.

Specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations that give them life and substance, which together create a zone of privacy protecting, here, the marital use of contraceptives from state prohibition.

entries.case: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
entries.held: When a statute administered by an agency is silent or ambiguous on the precise question, a court must defer to the agency's interpretation if it is a permissible construction of the statute. (Chevron was overruled by Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024).)
